### Introduction:

### Step 1. Import the necessary libraries

```{r step1, message=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# set the graphs to a cleaner style
theme_set(theme_classic())
```

### Step 2. Import the dataset from this [address](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/guipsamora/pandas_exercises/master/07_Visualization/Online_Retail/Online_Retail.csv).

### Step 3. Assign it to a variable called online_rt

Note: if you get strange characters, set `locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")` in `read_csv()`.

```{r}
# the same file is also included in this folder: read_csv("Online_Retail.csv", ...)
path <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/guipsamora/pandas_exercises/master/07_Visualization/Online_Retail/Online_Retail.csv"

online_rt <- read_csv(path, locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"))

head(online_rt)
```

### Step 4. Create a histogram with the 10 countries that have the most 'Quantity' ordered except UK

```{r}
# group by the Country
countries <- online_rt |>
  group_by(Country) |>
  summarise(Quantity = sum(Quantity)) |>
  # sort the value and get the first 10 after UK
  arrange(desc(Quantity)) |>
  slice(2:11)

# create the plot
ggplot(countries, aes(x = reorder(Country, -Quantity), y = Quantity)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Countries", y = "Quantity", title = "10 Countries with most orders") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5))
```

### Step 5. Exclude negative Quantity entries

```{r}
online_rt <- online_rt |> filter(Quantity > 0)
head(online_rt)
```

### Step 6. Create a scatterplot with the Quantity per UnitPrice by CustomerID for the top 3 Countries (except UK)

```{r}
# group by CustomerID and Country (rows without CustomerID are left out)
customers <- online_rt |>
  filter(!is.na(CustomerID)) |>
  group_by(CustomerID, Country) |>
  summarise(Quantity = sum(Quantity), UnitPrice = sum(UnitPrice), .groups = "drop") |>
  # there is an outlier with negative price
  filter(UnitPrice > 0)

# top three countries
top_countries <- c("Netherlands", "EIRE", "Germany")

# filter the data to just select the ones in top_countries
customers <- customers |> filter(Country %in% top_countries)

#################
# Graph Section #
#################

# facet_wrap() creates one panel per country (like seaborn's FacetGrid)
ggplot(customers, aes(x = Quantity, y = UnitPrice)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ Country)
```

### Step 7. Investigate why the previous results look so uninformative.

This section might seem a bit tedious to go through. But I've thought of it as some kind of a simulation of problems one might encounter when dealing with data and other people. Besides there is a prize at the end (i.e. Section 8).

(But feel free to jump right ahead into Section 8 if you want; it doesn't require that you finish this section.)

#### Step 7.1 Look at the first line of code in Step 6. And try to figure out if it leads to any kind of problem.

##### Step 7.1.1 Display the first few rows of that DataFrame.

```{r}
# This takes our initial data and groups it primarily by 'CustomerID' and secondarily by 'Country'.
# It sums the numeric columns under each group.
customers <- online_rt |>
  filter(!is.na(CustomerID)) |>
  group_by(CustomerID, Country) |>
  summarise(Quantity = sum(Quantity), UnitPrice = sum(UnitPrice), .groups = "drop")

# Here's what it looks like:
head(customers)
```

##### Step 7.1.2 Think about what that piece of code does and display the type of `UnitPrice`

```{r}
class(customers$UnitPrice)
# So it's numeric.
# But why did we sum 'UnitPrice', to begin with?
# If 'UnitPrice' wasn't something that we were interested in then it would be OK
# since we wouldn't care whether UnitPrice was being summed or not.
# But we want our graphs to reflect 'UnitPrice'!
# Note that summing up 'UnitPrice' can be highly misleading.
# It doesn't tell us much as to what the customer is doing.
# Suppose, a customer places one order of 1000 items that are worth $1 each.
# Another customer places a thousand orders of 1 item worth $1.
# There isn't much of a difference between what the former and the latter customers did.
# After all, they've spent the same amount of money.
# So we should be careful when we're summing columns. Sometimes we intend to sum just one column
# ('Quantity' in this case) and another column like UnitPrice gets into the mix.
```

##### Step 7.1.3 Pull data from `online_rt` for `CustomerID`s 12346 and 12347.

```{r}
online_rt |>
  filter(CustomerID == 12347) |>
  arrange(desc(UnitPrice)) |>
  head()

online_rt |>
  filter(CustomerID == 12346) |>
  arrange(desc(UnitPrice)) |>
  head()
# The result is exactly what we'd suspected. Customer 12346 placed
# one giant order, whereas 12347 placed a lot of smaller orders.
# So we've identified one potential reason why our plots looked so weird at section 6.
# At this stage we need to go back to the initial problem we've specified at section 6.
# And make it more precise.
```

#### Step 7.2 Reinterpreting the initial problem.

To reiterate the question that we were dealing with:
"Create a scatterplot with the Quantity per UnitPrice by CustomerID for the top 3 Countries"

The question is open to a set of different interpretations.
We need to disambiguate.

We could do a single plot by looking at all the data from the top 3 countries.
Or we could do one plot per country. To keep things consistent with the rest of the exercise,
let's stick to the latter option. So that's settled.

But "top 3 countries" with respect to what? Two answers suggest themselves:
Total sales volume (i.e. total quantity sold) or total sales (i.e. revenue).
This exercise goes for sales volume, so let's stick to that.

##### Step 7.2.1 Find out the top 3 countries in terms of sales volume.

```{r}
sales_volume <- online_rt |>
  group_by(Country) |>
  summarise(Quantity = sum(Quantity)) |>
  arrange(desc(Quantity))

top3 <- sales_volume$Country[2:4] # We are excluding UK
top3
```

##### Step 7.2.2

Now that we have the top 3 countries, we can focus on the rest of the problem:
"Quantity per UnitPrice by CustomerID".
We need to unpack that.

"by CustomerID" part is easy. That means we're going to be plotting one dot per CustomerID's on our plot. In other words, we're going to be grouping by CustomerID.

"Quantity per UnitPrice" is trickier. Here's what we know:
*One axis will represent a Quantity assigned to a given customer. This is easy; we can just plot the total Quantity for each customer.
*The other axis will represent a UnitPrice assigned to a given customer. Remember a single customer can have any number of orders with different prices, so summing up prices isn't quite helpful. Besides it's not quite clear what we mean when we say "unit price per customer"; it sounds like price of the customer! A reasonable alternative is that we assign each customer the average amount each has paid per item. So let's settle that question in that manner.

#### Step 7.3 Modify, select and plot data

##### Step 7.3.1 Add a column to online_rt called `Revenue` calculate the revenue (Quantity * UnitPrice) from each sale.

We will use this later to figure out an average price per customer.

```{r}
online_rt <- online_rt |> mutate(Revenue = Quantity * UnitPrice)
head(online_rt)
```

##### Step 7.3.2 Group by `CustomerID` and `Country` and find out the average price (`AvgPrice`) each customer spends per unit.

```{r}
plottable <- online_rt |>
  filter(Country %in% top3, !is.na(CustomerID)) |>
  group_by(CustomerID, Country) |>
  summarise(Quantity = sum(Quantity), Revenue = sum(Revenue), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(AvgPrice = Revenue / Quantity)

head(plottable)
```

##### Step 7.3.3 Plot

```{r}
####################
# Graph Section v 2#
####################

ggplot(plottable, aes(x = Quantity, y = AvgPrice)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ Country)
```

#### Step 7.4 What to do now?

We aren't much better-off than what we started with. The data are still extremely scattered around and don't seem quite informative.

But we shouldn't despair!
There are two things to realize:
1) The data seem to be skewed towards the axes (e.g. we don't have any values where Quantity = 50000 and AvgPrice = 5). So that might suggest a trend.
2) We have more data! We've only been looking at the data from 3 different countries and they are plotted on different graphs.

So: we should plot the data regardless of `Country` and hopefully see a less scattered graph.

##### Step 7.4.1 Plot the data for each `CustomerID` on a single graph

```{r}
plottable <- online_rt |>
  filter(!is.na(CustomerID)) |>
  group_by(CustomerID) |>
  summarise(Quantity = sum(Quantity), Revenue = sum(Revenue)) |>
  mutate(AvgPrice = Revenue / Quantity)

ggplot(plottable, aes(x = Quantity, y = AvgPrice)) +
  geom_point()

# Turns out the graph is still extremely skewed towards the axes like an exponential decay function.
```

##### Step 7.4.2 Zoom in so we can see that curve more clearly

```{r}
plottable <- online_rt |>
  filter(!is.na(CustomerID)) |>
  group_by(CustomerID, Country) |>
  summarise(Quantity = sum(Quantity), Revenue = sum(Revenue), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(AvgPrice = Revenue / Quantity)

ggplot(plottable, aes(x = Quantity, y = AvgPrice)) +
  geom_point() +
  # Zooming in. (I'm starting the axes from a negative value so that
  # the dots can be plotted in the graph completely.)
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-40, 2000), ylim = c(-1, 80))

# And there is still that pattern, this time in close-up!
```

### 8. Plot a line chart showing revenue (y) per UnitPrice (x).

Did Step 7 give us any insights about the data? Sure! As average price increases, the quantity ordered decreases. But that's hardly surprising. It would be surprising if that wasn't the case!

Nevertheless the rate of drop in quantity is so drastic, it makes me wonder how our revenue changes with respect to item price. It would not be that surprising if it didn't change that much. But it would be interesting to know whether most of our revenue comes from expensive or inexpensive items, and how that relation looks like.

That is what we are going to do now.

#### 8.1 Group `UnitPrice` by intervals of 1 for prices [0,50), and sum `Quantity` and `Revenue`.

```{r}
# These are the values for the graph.
# They are used both in selecting data from the table and plotting
# the data so I've assigned them to variables to increase consistency
# and make things easier when playing with the variables.
price_start <- 0
price_end <- 50
price_interval <- 1

# Creating the buckets to collect the data accordingly
buckets <- seq(price_start, price_end, by = price_interval)

# Select the data and sum
revenue_per_price <- online_rt |>
  filter(UnitPrice >= price_start, UnitPrice < price_end) |>
  mutate(price_bucket = cut(UnitPrice, buckets, right = FALSE)) |>
  group_by(price_bucket) |>
  summarise(Quantity = sum(Quantity), Revenue = sum(Revenue)) |>
  # the lower limit of each bucket, as a number, to use in the x axis
  mutate(price = buckets[as.integer(price_bucket)])

head(revenue_per_price)
```

#### 8.3 Plot.

```{r}
ggplot(revenue_per_price, aes(x = price, y = Revenue)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = paste0("Unit Price (in intervals of ", price_interval, ")"), y = "Revenue")
```

#### 8.4 Make it look nicer.

x-axis needs values.
y-axis isn't that easy to read; show in terms of millions.

```{r}
ggplot(revenue_per_price, aes(x = price, y = Revenue)) +
  geom_line() +
  # Place labels
  labs(x = paste0("Unit Price (in buckets of ", price_interval, ")"), y = "Revenue") +
  # Even though the data is bucketed in intervals of 1,
  # I'll plot ticks a little bit further apart from each other to avoid cluttering.
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(price_start, price_end, 3)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M"))

# Looks like a major chunk of our revenue comes from items worth $0-$3!
```
